content: Lay-led self-management education programs are increasingly being implemented to encourage self-care among individuals with chronic conditions. These programs are structured and delivered by non-clinician facilitators, often individuals who themselves have experience managing chronic conditions. The goal of this systematic review was to evaluate the effectiveness of such programs compared to no intervention or clinician-led programs. To conduct this review, a comprehensive search of multiple databases was performed, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, AMED, CINAHL, DARE, the National Research Register, the NHS Economic Evaluations Database, PsycINFO, and the Science Citation Index. The search covered studies published from January 1986 to mid-2006. Reference lists of included studies were also reviewed, and forward citation tracking was conducted. Investigators and experts in the field were contacted for additional information. No language restrictions were applied. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared structured lay-led self-management education programs for chronic conditions against either no intervention or clinician-led programs. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the trials and extracted data. Additional information was sought from study authors when necessary. The results of the RCTs were pooled using a random-effects model, with standardized mean differences (SMDs) or weighted mean differences (WMDs) calculated for continuous outcomes. Seventeen trials involving a total of 7,442 participants were included in the review. The interventions shared similar structures and components, but there was significant variability in the chronic conditions studied, the outcomes measured, and the effects observed. Notably, no studies included children or adolescents, only one study provided data on outcomes beyond six months, and only two studies reported clinical outcomes. Primary Outcomes: Health Status: There was a small but statistically significant reduction in pain (SMD -0.10, 95% CI -0.17 to -0.04), disability (SMD -0.15, 95% CI -0.25 to -0.05), and fatigue (SMD -0.16, 95% CI -0.23 to -0.09). Depression also showed a small statistically significant improvement (SMD -0.16, 95% CI -0.24 to -0.07). However, there was no statistically or clinically significant improvement in psychological well-being (SMD -0.12, 95% CI -0.33 to 0.09) or health-related quality of life (WMD -0.03, 95% CI -0.09 to 0.02). Six studies reported a statistically significant improvement in self-rated general health (WMD -0.20, 95% CI -0.31 to -0.10). Health Behaviors: Seven studies demonstrated a small but statistically significant increase in self-reported aerobic exercise (SMD -0.20, 95% CI -0.27 to -0.12). Four studies showed a moderate improvement in cognitive symptom management (WMD -0.55, 95% CI -0.85 to -0.26). Healthcare Utilization: There were no statistically significant differences between groups in terms of physician or general practitioner visits (SMD -0.03, 95% CI -0.09 to 0.04) or days/nights spent in the hospital (WMD -0.32, 95% CI -0.71 to 0.07). Self-Efficacy: Confidence in managing one’s condition showed a small but statistically significant improvement (SMD -0.30, 95% CI -0.41 to -0.19). No adverse events were reported in any of the included studies. Conclusions: Lay-led self-management education programs may result in small, short-term improvements in self-efficacy, self-rated health, cognitive symptom management, and the frequency of aerobic exercise. However, there is no evidence to suggest that these programs lead to significant improvements in psychological health, symptoms, or health-related quality of life, nor do they appear to significantly impact healthcare utilization. Future research should focus on evaluating the long-term outcomes of these interventions, their effects on clinical measures of disease, and their potential applicability to children and adolescents.
